sense: of food and farming: grown without artificial chemicals

terms.grammar: phrase: the participle of colō, agreeing with the food
evidence: M-O s.v. pesticide: venēnum insectīs internecīvum (Egger)
terms.comment: No reference work has a Latin word for organic food (Morgan–Owens gives only the modern languages’ words). A plain description: venēnum, any strong drug or poison, is the pesticide (Morgan–Owens, after Egger), and cultus is “grown, farmed”.

evidence: M-O s.v. organic (of food): Fr. biologique, It. biologico
Levi–Bini p. 10, s.v. biologico: ad animantium vītae pertinēns
terms.comment: The Greek-formed word of the modern languages’ “bio” food; Levi & Bini render “biological” by a phrase, “belonging to the life of living things”, and give the word only for the biologist, biologus. Clear to a European listener, but a label, not a description.
Classically “of instruments”: mechanical, or musical (Lewis & Short); modern Latin uses it for organic in the sense of living matter (M-O s.v. organic), never of food.

phrases.latin: Haec māla sine venēnīs culta sunt.

sources: Lewis & Short: venenum · Lewis & Short: colo · Lewis & Short: organicus
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. organic; s.v. pesticide.
Enrico Levi and Arturo Bini, Il latino come lingua viva (1937), p. 10, s.v. biologico.
